claim: Salpingoeca rosetta is one of the closest living relatives of animals.
source: In one of the closest living relatives of animals, the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta, we find that rosette colony development is induced by the prey bacterium Algoriphagus machipongonensis and its close relatives in the Bacteroidetes phylum.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction regarding choanoflagellate phylogeny.

claim: Rosette colony development in Salpingoeca rosetta is induced by the prey bacterium Algoriphagus machipongonensis.
source: In one of the closest living relatives of animals, the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta, we find that rosette colony development is induced by the prey bacterium Algoriphagus machipongonensis and its close relatives in the Bacteroidetes phylum.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in figures and described in results.

claim: Close relatives of Algoriphagus machipongonensis in the Bacteroidetes phylum can induce rosette colony development in S. rosetta.
source: In one of the closest living relatives of animals, the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta, we find that rosette colony development is induced by the prey bacterium Algoriphagus machipongonensis and its close relatives in the Bacteroidetes phylum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Table 1 and Figure 2 showing multiple Bacteroidetes species inducing colony formation.

claim: RIF-1 is a rosette inducing factor produced by A. machipongonensis that belongs to the class of sulfonolipids.
source: Here we show that a rosette inducing factor (RIF-1) produced by A. machipongonensis belongs to the small class of sulfonolipids, obscure relatives of the better known sphingolipids that play important roles in signal transmission in plants, animals, and fungi.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by biochemical characterization data including MS and NMR analysis.

claim: Sulfonolipids are obscure relatives of sphingolipids.
source: Here we show that a rosette inducing factor (RIF-1) produced by A. machipongonensis belongs to the small class of sulfonolipids, obscure relatives of the better known sphingolipids that play important roles in signal transmission in plants, animals, and fungi.
evidence: This is based on established chemical knowledge about the relationship between sulfonolipids and sphingolipids.

claim: Sphingolipids play important roles in signal transmission in plants, animals, and fungi.
source: Here we show that a rosette inducing factor (RIF-1) produced by A. machipongonensis belongs to the small class of sulfonolipids, obscure relatives of the better known sphingolipids that play important roles in signal transmission in plants, animals, and fungi.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about sphingolipid function.

claim: RIF-1 has extraordinary potency at femtomolar (10^-15 M) concentrations.
source: RIF-1 has extraordinary potency (femtomolar, or 10−15 M) and S. rosetta can respond to it over a broad dynamic range—nine orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 4.

claim: S. rosetta can respond to RIF-1 over a broad dynamic range of nine orders of magnitude.
source: RIF-1 has extraordinary potency (femtomolar, or 10−15 M) and S. rosetta can respond to it over a broad dynamic range—nine orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 4.

claim: This study provides a prototypical example of bacterial sulfonolipids triggering eukaryotic morphogenesis.
source: This study provides a prototypical example of bacterial sulfonolipids triggering eukaryotic morphogenesis and suggests molecular mechanisms through which bacteria may have contributed to the evolution of animals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Bacteria may have contributed to the evolution of animals through molecular mechanisms involving sulfonolipids.
source: This study provides a prototypical example of bacterial sulfonolipids triggering eukaryotic morphogenesis and suggests molecular mechanisms through which bacteria may have contributed to the evolution of animals.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the study's findings and the evolutionary relationship between choanoflagellates and animals.

claim: Choanoflagellates are the closest living relatives of animals.
source: Choanoflagellates, microscopic bacteria-eating eukaryotes that are the closest living relatives of animals (James-Clark 1868; Saville Kent 1880; Hibberd 1975; Carr et al. 2008; King et al. 2008; Ruiz-Trillo et al. 2008), could provide particularly important insights into the mechanisms underlying bacterial influences on animal biology and evolution.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Some choanoflagellates have both solitary and multicellular stages in their life histories.
source: Moreover, some choanoflagellates have both solitary and multicellular stages in their life histories (Leadbeater 1983; Karpov and Coupe 1998; Dayel et al. 2011) and understanding the environmental cues that regulate choanoflagellate colony formation could provide a molecular model for animal multicellularity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies of choanoflagellate life cycles.

claim: In S. rosetta, rosette-shaped multicellular colonies develop when a single founder cell undergoes multiple rounds of incomplete cytokinesis.
source: In the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta, rosette-shaped multicellular colonies develop when a single founder cell undergoes multiple rounds of incomplete cytokinesis, leaving neighboring cells physically attached by fine intercellular bridges (Fairclough et al. 2010; Dayel et al. 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing the developmental mechanism.

claim: Neighboring cells in S. rosetta rosette colonies are physically attached by fine intercellular bridges.
source: In the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta, rosette-shaped multicellular colonies develop when a single founder cell undergoes multiple rounds of incomplete cytokinesis, leaving neighboring cells physically attached by fine intercellular bridges (Fairclough et al. 2010; Dayel et al. 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing the cellular structure.

claim: Laboratory cultures of S. rosetta ATCC50818 consistently produced single cells, with small numbers of rosette colonies forming only sporadically.
source: Although the original stock of S. rosetta (ATCC50818) was established from a rosette colony (Dayel et al. 2011), laboratory cultures consistently produced single cells, with small numbers of rosette colonies forming only sporadically (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of ATCC50818 culture with an antibiotic cocktail resulted in a culture line (RCA) that never formed rosette colonies.
source: Treatment of the ATCC50818 culture with an antibiotic cocktail resulted in a culture of S. rosetta cells that proliferated robustly by feeding on the remaining antibiotic-resistant bacteria but never formed rosette colonies, even upon removal of antibiotics (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: S. rosetta cells in the RCA culture remained competent to form colonies when stimulated by the original community of environmental bacteria.
source: Supplementation of RCA cultures with bacteria from ATCC50818 restored rosette colony development, revealing that S. rosetta cells in the RCA culture remained competent to form colonies and would do so when stimulated by the original community of environmental bacteria.
evidence: This is an experimental finding demonstrating that the cells retained developmental competence.

claim: Addition of A. machipongonensis to RCA cultures was sufficient to induce rosette development.
source: Addition of A. machipongonensis to RCA cultures was sufficient to induce rosette development.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1C and supported by the image.

claim: Of 64 bacterial isolates from ATCC50818 tested, only A. machipongonensis induced rosette colony development in the RCA cell line.
source: To determine which co-isolated bacterial species stimulate rosette colony development in S. rosetta, the RCA cell line was supplemented with 64 independent bacterial isolates from ATCC50818 and monitored for the appearance of rosette colonies. Only one bacterial species from ATCC50818, the previously undescribed Algoriphagus machipongonensis (phylum Bacteroidetes; Alegado et al. 2012), induced rosette colony development in the RCA cell line (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from screening bacterial isolates.

claim: S. rosetta cultures fed solely with A. machipongonensis yielded high percentages of rosette colonies.
source: S. rosetta cultures fed solely with A. machipongonensis yielded high percentages of rosette colonies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that no other co-isolated bacterial species is required to stimulate rosette colony development.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No other co-isolated bacterial species is required to stimulate rosette colony development in S. rosetta.
source: S. rosetta cultures fed solely with A. machipongonensis yielded high percentages of rosette colonies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that no other co-isolated bacterial species is required to stimulate rosette colony development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing A. machipongonensis alone is sufficient.

claim: All 15 Algoriphagus species tested induced rosette colony development in S. rosetta.
source: In contrast, all 15 Algoriphagus species tested induced rosette colony development, as did six of 16 other closely related species tested in the Bacteroidetes phylum (Table 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Six of 16 other closely related species tested in the Bacteroidetes phylum induced rosette colony development in S. rosetta.
source: In contrast, all 15 Algoriphagus species tested induced rosette colony development, as did six of 16 other closely related species tested in the Bacteroidetes phylum (Table 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

claim: None of the non-Bacteroidetes species tested were competent to induce rosette colony development in S. rosetta.
source: None of the non-Bacteroidetes species tested, including members of the γ-proteobacteria, α-proteobacteria, and Gram-positive bacteria, were competent to induce rosette colony development.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: The ability to induce rosette colony development is enriched in Algoriphagus bacteria and their relatives.
source: Therefore, the ability to induce rosette colony development is enriched in Algoriphagus bacteria and their relatives.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic distribution of inducing activity shown in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: RIF activity was present in conditioned medium from A. machipongonensis, even when grown in the absence of choanoflagellates.
source: Preliminary studies demonstrated that RIF activity was present in conditioned medium from A. machipongonensis, even when grown in the absence of choanoflagellates.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from preliminary biochemical studies.

claim: RIF activity was found in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope.
source: Furthermore, the activity was also found in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope and was heat, protease, and nuclease resistant, revealing that the compound is not a protein, RNA, or DNA (Table 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Table 2.

claim: RIF activity is heat resistant.
source: Furthermore, the activity was also found in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope and was heat, protease, and nuclease resistant, revealing that the compound is not a protein, RNA, or DNA (Table 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Table 2.

claim: RIF activity is protease resistant.
source: Furthermore, the activity was also found in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope and was heat, protease, and nuclease resistant, revealing that the compound is not a protein, RNA, or DNA (Table 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Table 2.

claim: RIF activity is nuclease resistant.
source: Furthermore, the activity was also found in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope and was heat, protease, and nuclease resistant, revealing that the compound is not a protein, RNA, or DNA (Table 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Table 2.

claim: The RIF compound is not a protein, RNA, or DNA.
source: Furthermore, the activity was also found in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope and was heat, protease, and nuclease resistant, revealing that the compound is not a protein, RNA, or DNA (Table 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the resistance to heat, protease, and nuclease treatments.

claim: Neither LPS nor PGN from A. machipongonensis triggered rosette development, alone or in combination.
source: The bacterial cell envelope components lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and peptidoglycan (PGN) from Gram-negative bacteria have long been known to affect host biology (Cohn and Morse 1960; Hoffmann et al. 1999; Kopp and Medzhitov 1999; Takeuchi et al. 1999; Medzhitov and Janeway 2000; Kimbrell and Beutler 2001; Koropatnick et al. 2004), but neither LPS nor PGN from A. machipongonensis triggered rosette development, alone or in combination (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: A. machipongonensis crude lipid extracts enriched in sphingolipids robustly induced rosette development.
source: Instead, we found that A. machipongonensis crude lipid extracts enriched in sphingolipids robustly induced rosette development (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: In animals, sphingolipid signaling pathways regulate developmental processes such as cell death, survival, differentiation, and migration.
source: In animals, sphingolipid signaling pathways regulate developmental processes such as cell death, survival, differentiation, and migration (Prieschl and Baumruker 2000; Pyne and Pyne 2000; Spiegel and Milstien 2000; Hannun et al. 2001; Merrill et al. 2001; Herr et al. 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sphingolipids serve essential functions both as structural components of cell membranes and as signaling molecules in diverse eukaryotes.
source: Moreover, sphingolipids serve essential functions both as structural components of cell membranes and as signaling molecules in diverse eukaryotes (Hannich et al. 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The phylogenetic distribution of sphingolipids in bacteria is largely limited to Bacteroidetes and Sphingomonas.
source: In contrast, the phylogenetic distribution of sphingolipids in bacteria is largely limited to Bacteroidetes and Sphingomonas, where their endogenous functions are poorly understood (Olsen and Jantzen 2001; An et al. 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RIF-1 has a molecular formula of C32H64NO7S.
source: Based on high-resolution mass spectrometry, RIF-1 has a molecular formula of C32H64NO7S (M-H: exptl. 606.44027, calcd. 606.44035, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is determined by high-resolution mass spectrometry data.

claim: RIF-1 represents only 0.015% of the A. machipongonensis sphingolipid pool.
source: RIF-1 represents only 0.015% of the A. machipogonensis sphingolipid pool.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the purification process.

claim: RIF-1 is an unusual sulfonolipid with the structure 3,5-dihydroxy-2-(2-hydroxy-13-methyltetradecanamido)-15-methylhexadecane-1-sulfonic acid.
source: Detailed analysis of one- and two-dimensional (COSY, HMBC, TOCSY, Figure 3—figure supplements 3–15) nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, 600 MHz, Table 3) spectra revealed the planar structure of RIF-1, an unusual sulfonolipid shown in Figure 3B.
evidence: This is determined by detailed NMR spectroscopic analysis.

claim: In sphingolipids, a sphingoid base (1,3-dihydroxy-2-aminoalkane) is linked through an amide bond to a fatty acid.
source: In sphingolipids, a sphingoid base (1,3-dihydroxy-2-aminoalkane) is linked through an amide bond to a fatty acid.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge about sphingolipid structure.

claim: In RIF-1, a capnoid base (2-amino-3-hydroxy-15-methyl-1-sulfonic acid) replaces the sphingoid base.
source: In RIF-1, a capnoid base (2-amino-3-hydroxy-15-methyl-1-sulfonic acid) replaces the sphingoid base, and the sphingolipid hydroxyl, which is the attachment point for the major diversifying elements of the sphingolipid family, is replaced by a sulfonic acid.
evidence: This is a structural characterization based on NMR and MS data.

claim: The sphingolipid hydroxyl in RIF-1 is replaced by a sulfonic acid.
source: In RIF-1, a capnoid base (2-amino-3-hydroxy-15-methyl-1-sulfonic acid) replaces the sphingoid base, and the sphingolipid hydroxyl, which is the attachment point for the major diversifying elements of the sphingolipid family, is replaced by a sulfonic acid.
evidence: This is a structural characterization based on NMR and MS data.

claim: Commercial sphingolipids (sphingomyelin, monosiloganglioside, galactocerebroside, and N-palmitoyl-DL-dihydrolacto cerebroside) failed to show any activity in the rosette colony induction assay.
source: Significantly, commercial sphingolipids (sphingomyelin, monosiloganglioside, galactocerebroside, and N-palmitoyl-DL-dihydrolacto cerebroside; Table 2) failed to show any activity in our assay system.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Table 2.

claim: RIF-1 is the first sulfonolipid demonstrated to influence developmental processes in eukaryotes.
source: To our knowledge, RIF-1 is the first sulfonolipid demonstrated to influence developmental processes in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Purified RIF-1 induces rosette formation with a bell-shaped dose-response curve over a broad range of concentrations, from 10^-2 to 10^7 fM.
source: Purified RIF-1 induces rosette formation with a bell-shaped dose-response curve over a broad range of concentrations, from 10−2 to 107 fM or some nine orders of magnitude (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by dose-response data in Figure 4.

claim: No observable effects of RIF-1 were seen below 10^-5 fM.
source: No observable effects were seen below 10−5 fM, and RIF-1 appears to be inactive above 108 fM.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the dose-response study.

claim: RIF-1 appears to be inactive above 10^8 fM.
source: No observable effects were seen below 10−5 fM, and RIF-1 appears to be inactive above 108 fM.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the dose-response study.

claim: A. machipongonensis conditioned medium contains 10^4 fM RIF-1.
source: A. machipongonensis conditioned medium contains 104 fM RIF-1 (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3), and even if this conditioned medium measurement exaggerates natural concentrations by a factor of 106, S. rosetta could still respond to its presence.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement supported by LC-MS data in Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The shape of the dose-response curve and the potency of RIF-1 suggest that S. rosetta perceives RIF-1 in a manner consistent with a receptor-ligand interaction.
source: The shape of the dose-response curve and the potency of RIF-1 suggest that S. rosetta perceives RIF-1 in a manner consistent with a receptor-ligand interaction, albeit a receptor of exquisite sensitivity and remarkable dynamic range.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dose-response data.

claim: The maximal activity of pure RIF-1 (5.6 ± 0.5% colonial cells/total cells) differs from that of the sphingolipid-enriched lipid fraction (19.2 ± 4.6% colonial cells/total cells).
source: While RIF-1 is the only molecule detected with rosette-inducing activity, its maximal activity (5.6 ± 0.5% colonial cells/total cells) differs from that of the sphingolipid-enriched lipid fraction (19.2 ± 4.6% colonial cells/total cells; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of experimental data.

claim: The difference in maximal activity between pure RIF-1 and the lipid fraction may be due to delivery issues of the purified and highly hydrophobic molecule.
source: This difference may be due to delivery issues of the purified and highly hydrophobic molecule, which in nature resides in membranes and potentially in membrane vesicles.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in activity.

claim: The full potency of RIF-1 as an inducer of colony development may require additional A. machipongonensis molecules not identified in this study.
source: Alternatively, the full potency of RIF-1 as an inducer of colony development may require additional A. machipongonensis molecules not identified in this study.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed difference in activity.

claim: The ecological relevance of RIF-1 signaling is indicated by the coexistence of S. rosetta and A. machipongonensis in nature.
source: The ecological relevance of this signaling interaction is indicated both by the coexistence of S. rosetta and A. machipongonensis in nature and by the fact that the activity of RIF-1 at femtomolar concentrations makes it markedly more potent than other marine signaling molecules [e.g., Vibrio autoinducer (Schaefer et al. 1996) and the tripeptide pheromones of the Caribbean spiny lobster (Ziegler and Forward 2007)].
evidence: This is an inference based on the natural co-occurrence of the organisms.

claim: RIF-1 at femtomolar concentrations is markedly more potent than other marine signaling molecules such as Vibrio autoinducer and the tripeptide pheromones of the Caribbean spiny lobster.
source: The ecological relevance of this signaling interaction is indicated both by the coexistence of S. rosetta and A. machipongonensis in nature and by the fact that the activity of RIF-1 at femtomolar concentrations makes it markedly more potent than other marine signaling molecules [e.g., Vibrio autoinducer (Schaefer et al. 1996) and the tripeptide pheromones of the Caribbean spiny lobster (Ziegler and Forward 2007)].
evidence: This is a comparison based on the measured potency of RIF-1 and cited potencies of other molecules.

claim: The potency of RIF-1 signaling compares favorably with that of silkworm moth sex pheromone signaling.
source: The potency of RIF-1 signaling compares favorably with that of silkworm moth sex pheromone signaling, in which vapors from an ∼4 fM solution of bombykol, the sex pheromone of the silkworm moth, induce a pronounced wing fluttering response in males (Butenandt et al. 1961; Agosta 1992; Roelofs 1995).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the measured potency of RIF-1 and cited potency of bombykol.

claim: A. machipongonensis cell density, as revealed by RIF-1 concentration, provides S. rosetta with an indication of conditions under which rosette colony development would be advantageous.
source: Therefore we favor a model in which A. machipongonensis cell density, as revealed by RIF-1 concentration, provides S. rosetta with an indication of conditions under which rosette colony development would be advantageous, for instance by promoting more efficient capture of planktonic bacteria (Kreft 2010).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and cited ecological reasoning.

claim: Rosette colony development may promote more efficient capture of planktonic bacteria.
source: Therefore we favor a model in which A. machipongonensis cell density, as revealed by RIF-1 concentration, provides S. rosetta with an indication of conditions under which rosette colony development would be advantageous, for instance by promoting more efficient capture of planktonic bacteria (Kreft 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to ecological reasoning.

claim: The ability of S. rosetta to respond to increasing bacterial cell density likely requires the hypothesized RIF-1 receptor to become less sensitive at higher concentrations.
source: In analogy to the chemotaxis system of bacteria (Falke et al. 1997), the ability of S. rosetta to respond to increasing bacterial cell density likely requires the hypothesized RIF-1 receptor to become less sensitive at higher concentrations.
evidence: This is an inference based on analogy to bacterial chemotaxis systems.

claim: The presence of RIF-1 in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope suggests that it may be encountered by S. rosetta during phagocytosis.
source: Although the presence of RIF-1 in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope suggests that it may be encountered by S. rosetta during phagocytosis, it can also function at a distance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization of RIF-1 in the bacterial cell envelope.

claim: RIF-1 can function at a distance.
source: Although the presence of RIF-1 in the A. machipongonensis cell envelope suggests that it may be encountered by S. rosetta during phagocytosis, it can also function at a distance.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-response data showing activity at very low concentrations.

claim: RIF-1 may be released into the environment in membrane vesicles.
source: We hypothesize that RIF-1 may be released into the environment in membrane vesicles, which have been described in Gram-negative bacteria such as Bacteroidetes (Zhou et al. 1998; Møller et al. 2005), and that additional membrane constituents might be required for the full potency of RIF-1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known mechanisms of lipid release in bacteria.

claim: Additional membrane constituents might be required for the full potency of RIF-1.
source: We hypothesize that RIF-1 may be released into the environment in membrane vesicles, which have been described in Gram-negative bacteria such as Bacteroidetes (Zhou et al. 1998; Møller et al. 2005), and that additional membrane constituents might be required for the full potency of RIF-1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the difference in activity between pure RIF-1 and the lipid fraction.

claim: Bacterially-produced sphingolipids in general, and sulfonolipids in particular, may be essential for the chemical signaling that allows Bacteroidetes to influence cell differentiation and morphogenesis in diverse animals.
source: The morphogenetic interaction described here between S. rosetta and A. machipongonensis raises the possibility that bacterially-produced sphingolipids in general, and sulfonolipids in particular, may be essential for the chemical signaling that allows Bacteroidetes to influence cell differentiation and morphogenesis in diverse animals (Falkow 2006; Mazmanian et al. 2008; Lee and Mazmanian 2010; An et al. 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the findings, supported by citations to related work.

claim: Sulfobacins A and B were isolated from the culture broth of a Chryseobacterium sp. and reported as von Willebrand factor receptor antagonists.
source: Sulfobacins A and B, which were isolated from the culture broth of a Chryseobacterium sp. were reported as von Willebrand factor receptor antagonists, and flavocristamide A, from a related bacterial species, was reported as a DNA polymerase α inhibitor (Kamiyama et al. 1995a; Kobayashi et al. 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Flavocristamide A, from a related bacterial species, was reported as a DNA polymerase α inhibitor.
source: Sulfobacins A and B, which were isolated from the culture broth of a Chryseobacterium sp. were reported as von Willebrand factor receptor antagonists, and flavocristamide A, from a related bacterial species, was reported as a DNA polymerase α inhibitor (Kamiyama et al. 1995a; Kobayashi et al. 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The connection between Bacteroidetes and animal development may have deep evolutionary roots.
source: The pervasiveness of interactions between Bacteroidetes and animals (Webster et al. 2004; Wexler 2007), coupled with the close evolutionary relationship between choanoflagellates and animals (King and Carroll 2001; King 2004; King et al. 2008; Ruiz-Trillo et al. 2008), raise the possibility that the connection between Bacteroidetes and animal development has deep evolutionary roots (McFall-Ngai 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on phylogenetic relationships and the pervasiveness of Bacteroidetes-animal interactions.

claim: The discovery of RIF-1 and its biological activity toward S. rosetta provides both the molecular basis and model organism for further understanding a new and potentially important class of small molecule information transfer.
source: The discovery of RIF-1 and its biological activity toward S. rosetta provides both the molecular basis and model organism for further understanding a new and potentially important class of small molecule information transfer.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Approximately 700 µg of active RIF-1 compound was obtained from 160 L of A. machipongonensis culture.
source: RIF activity tracked with a single fraction, which was further purified by several rounds of preparative thin-layer chromatography (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) to yield approximately 700 µg of active compound (RIF-1) with sufficient purity for structural analysis.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the purification process.

claim: S. rosetta rosette colonies contain clusters of at least four closely associated cells with organized polarity.
source: S. rosetta rosette colonies can be distinguished from other cell types in that they contain clusters of at least four closely associated cells with organized polarity; each cell oriented with its flagellum pointing outward from a central focus.
evidence: This is a morphological description used as a criterion for identifying rosette colonies.

claim: In S. rosetta rosette colonies, each cell is oriented with its flagellum pointing outward from a central focus.
source: S. rosetta rosette colonies can be distinguished from other cell types in that they contain clusters of at least four closely associated cells with organized polarity; each cell oriented with its flagellum pointing outward from a central focus.
evidence: This is a morphological description used as a criterion for identifying rosette colonies.

claim: Bacteroidetes bacteria regulate morphogenetic processes in diverse lineages including animals, red algae, and green algae.
source: Although Bacteroidetes bacteria regulate morphogenetic processes in such diverse lineages as animals, red algae, and green algae (Provasoli and Pintner 1980; Matsuo et al. 2005; Mazmanian et al. 2005), the bacterially produced chemical cues that regulate most of these partnerships remain obscure.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The bacterially produced chemical cues that regulate most Bacteroidetes partnerships remain obscure.
source: Although Bacteroidetes bacteria regulate morphogenetic processes in such diverse lineages as animals, red algae, and green algae (Provasoli and Pintner 1980; Matsuo et al. 2005; Mazmanian et al. 2005), the bacterially produced chemical cues that regulate most of these partnerships remain obscure.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.
